section.title: The Temptation in the Wilderness
section.sectionRationale: Immediately after the Father declares Jesus His beloved Son, the Spirit leads Him into the wilderness to be tested by the devil. Three times the tempter attacks, and three times Jesus answers with Scripture. Where Adam fell in a garden and Israel failed in the desert, the true Son stands firm, proving Himself the faithful Israel and the obedient Son before His ministry unfolds.
section.thesis: In the wilderness the beloved Son is tested to the limit and, by trusting and obeying the word of God, defeats the tempter at every point, succeeding where Adam and Israel failed, and refusing every shortcut to glory that bypasses the path of obedient suffering.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the Spirit leads Jesus to be tested after forty days of fasting; the temptation to turn stones to bread; the temptation to leap from the temple; the temptation to gain the kingdoms by worshiping Satan; and the devil's defeat.

verses.text: Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be {{peirazo|tempted}} by the {{diabolos|devil}}.
After fasting forty days and forty nights, He was hungry.

units.label: Bread from stones
units.note: man shall not live on bread alone

verses.text: The tempter came to Him and said, “If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.”
But Jesus answered, “{{gegraptai|It is written}}: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”

units.label: The pinnacle of the temple
units.note: do not put the Lord to the test

verses.text: Then the devil took Him to the holy city and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple.

“If You are the Son of God,” he said, “throw Yourself down. For it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning You, and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.’”
Jesus replied, “It is also written: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

units.label: All the kingdoms of the world
units.note: worship the Lord your God and serve Him only

verses.text: Again, the devil took Him to a very high mountain and showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.
“All this I will give You,” he said, “if You will fall down and worship me.”
“Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘{{proskyneo|Worship}} the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”
Then the devil left Him, and angels came and ministered to Him.

peirazo.gloss: To test, try, tempt. The same word covers a testing meant to prove and a tempting meant to destroy. The Spirit leads Jesus to be tested, and the devil means it for ruin, yet the trial proves the Son faithful.

diabolos.gloss: Devil, slanderer, accuser. The personal enemy of God and His people, also named Satan in the passage. He tempts with half-truths and even misused Scripture, seeking to divert the Son from the Father's path.

gegraptai.gloss: It stands written, a perfect form meaning it was written and remains in force. Jesus meets each temptation with this settled authority, answering all three times from Deuteronomy, the very book Israel had in the wilderness.

proskyneo.gloss: To worship, bow down, do homage. The devil demands the worship due to God alone; Jesus answers that worship and service belong to the Lord only, refusing to win the world by any means but the Father's.

basic.context: Straight from the joy of His baptism, Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness and tested by the devil for forty days. Weak with hunger, He faces three temptations: to make bread from stones, to leap from the temple and force God to catch Him, and to gain all the world's kingdoms by worshiping Satan. Each time Jesus answers with a verse from Deuteronomy, and the devil finally leaves.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this against the background of the Old Testament. Jesus' forty days recall Israel's forty years in the desert, and He quotes the very passages Israel learned there. Where Israel grumbled, tested God, and turned to idols, Jesus trusts, obeys, and worships God alone. He is the true Israel and the faithful Son, undoing the pattern of failure.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is tested, a word that can mean both a trial to prove and a temptation to destroy; the Spirit intends the first, the devil the second. Each answer begins it is written, a settled, standing authority. And Jesus insists that worship belongs to God alone, refusing the devil's offer to gain the world by bowing to him.
basic.typology: Jesus is the new Adam, tempted as Adam was but standing firm where Adam fell. He is the true Israel, forty days in the wilderness matching forty years, succeeding where the nation failed. And He is the obedient Son, tested as God's son Israel was tested, proving faithful to the Father's word and way.
basic.christ: The whole passage displays Christ's perfect obedience and His victory over the devil. He refuses every shortcut to messianic glory, choosing the Father's path of suffering over the tempter's easy crown. His triumph here begins the rescue of a people held captive by the one He defeats, and His sinless obedience is part of the righteousness He wins for us.
basic.god: God is worthy of exclusive worship and trust. His word is the food by which His people truly live, and it is not to be twisted or put to the test. The Father sends His Son into the trial and sustains Him, and afterward sends angels to minister to Him, showing His care in the midst of testing.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:16, and 6:13 are the three texts Jesus quotes. Genesis 3 tells of Adam's fall to a similar temptation. Hebrews 4 says Jesus was tempted in every way yet without sin. And James 4 urges believers to resist the devil, who will flee.
basic.oneStory: In the wilderness the long story of human failure meets its turning point. Where Adam fell and Israel faltered, the beloved Son stands firm, armed with nothing but the word of God and unwavering trust in His Father. By refusing the tempter's shortcuts, Jesus sets His face toward the cross, the true and costly road to the kingdom, and begins to reclaim the world the devil claimed to own.

context.literary:
Matthew builds the temptation as a hinge. Behind it stands the baptism, where a voice from heaven says, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 3:17. Ahead lies the Sermon on the Mount. The devil's opening words in verses 3 and 6, 'If You are the Son of God,' pick up that very sentence and try to pry it open, so the whole scene is a test of what the Father has just said.

The account has a tidy shape. Verses 1 and 2 set the stage, three exchanges follow, and verse 11 closes the frame, with the Spirit who led Jesus in answered by angels who serve Him at the end. Each exchange has the same three beats: a proposal from the devil, an answer from Jesus introduced by Scripture, and a move to a new place, the desert, the holy city, the mountain. The settings climb, from low wilderness to temple height to the highest peak, and the stakes climb with them, from a private appetite, to a public spectacle, to a claim over everything.

Notice how the speech changes. In the first two rounds Jesus quotes Scripture and the devil replies by quoting Scripture back. By the third round the devil has stopped quoting and simply offers a bargain, and Jesus responds with a command, 'Away from Me, Satan!', before the final quotation. The little word 'then' (Matthew's habit of linking scenes) strings the movements together and keeps the reader moving toward the closing line, where the devil leaves.

All three answers come from a single stretch of Deuteronomy, chapters 6 to 8, Moses' sermon to Israel about what the forty years in the wilderness were for. Matthew is telling us how to read the scene: this is Israel's wilderness story told again, with a Son who passes the test.
context.historical:
The wilderness Matthew means is most likely the barren Judean desert that falls away from the hill country toward the Jordan and the Dead Sea. It is a land of limestone, wadis and little water, and the old tradition that points to the hills above Jericho is only a tradition. What matters for the first readers is its place in memory: it was where Israel had been formed, where Moses had met God, and where later prophets expected the LORD to act again. Many Jews of Jesus' day looked for a new deliverance that would begin in the desert.

Fasting for forty days was not an unknown feat in Israel's story. Moses was on the mountain with the LORD 'forty days and forty nights without eating bread or drinking water,' Exodus 34:28, and Elijah walked 'forty days and forty nights' to Horeb, 1 Kings 19:8. A Jewish reader would hear both of them in Matthew 4:2, and would hear Israel's forty years as well.

The holy city and the temple were the centre of Jewish worship, and the 'pinnacle' was a high point of the temple complex. Many identify it with the southeast corner above the Kidron Valley, where a long drop was visible, though the Greek word simply means a small wing, and we cannot be sure which corner is meant. The quotation from Psalm 91 fits the setting well, since that psalm pictured the faithful being kept safe by angels, and some people in Jesus' day expected the Messiah to appear dramatically at the temple.

The mountain offers 'all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.' In a world ruled by Rome, whose emperors claimed worship, the offer was as political as it was spiritual. Many first readers longed for a king who would break the pagan yoke; the devil proposes to hand Jesus that kingdom at once.
context.canonical:
The temptation is one of the Bible's great echo scenes. It answers Genesis 3. There a serpent questioned what God had said and a man and woman who were surrounded by plenty took what was forbidden; here the tempter faces a hungry man in a desert, and the outcome reverses. Paul draws the line from Adam's disobedience to Christ's obedience, 'so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19.

It also answers Israel's wilderness. God called Israel 'My firstborn son,' Exodus 4:22, and Hosea says 'out of Egypt I called My son,' Hosea 11:1, a line Matthew has already applied to Jesus in Matthew 2:15. Israel was tested in the desert and failed, quarrelling at Massah, Exodus 17:7, and demanding food they craved, Psalm 78:18. Paul warns the church not to 'test Christ, as some of them did,' 1 Corinthians 10:9. Jesus passes where they did not.

The other Gospels tell the story differently. Mark compresses it into two verses and adds that Jesus 'was with the wild animals,' Mark 1:12-13. Luke reverses the order of the second and third temptations so that the temple comes last, Luke 4:1-13, and adds that the devil 'left Him until an opportune time,' Luke 4:13.

The rest of the New Testament reads the scene as the opening of a war. Jesus' later words about tying up the strong man, Matthew 12:29, look back to it. The same lines of temptation return at the cross, where passers-by shout, 'If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!' Matthew 27:40, and in Gethsemane, where He says He could call on more than twelve legions of angels, Matthew 26:53. Hebrews says He 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wrote for readers who already believed Jesus was the Messiah and needed to understand what kind of Messiah He was. The temptation answers a puzzling question: if He is the Son of God, why does He go hungry, refuse miracles on demand and turn down a crown? Each refusal is a lesson in the character of His sonship. A Son does not use His power to serve Himself, does not force the Father's hand, and does not take glory by a road that avoids the Father's will.

Matthew also meant to give his hearers a pattern for their own testing. Jesus does not answer with a clever argument or a show of strength. He answers with what God has already said, and He takes the devil's misuse of Scripture as a reason to read Scripture more carefully, not less. The people of Matthew's day, who were pressed by Rome and tempted to seek deliverance by short cuts, were meant to see the same three choices set before them: provision on their own terms, proof of God's care on demand, or power by compromise.

Above all, Matthew wanted Israel's long failure to be seen as answered. The reader who knows Deuteronomy 6 to 8 hears that the Son has finally done what the nation could not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a unique event, the testing of the Messiah, and does not command believers to go into a desert and fast for forty days or to expect the same three temptations in the same form. It describes who Jesus is and what He did. Where it does speak to us is in the way He resists. It is instruction by example, and the New Testament itself invites the connection, since Hebrews 2:18 says that because He suffered when tempted, He is able to help those who are tempted.

Care is needed in applying the three answers. 'Man shall not live on bread alone' does not make eating wrong, nor does it forbid asking God for bread, as Matthew 6:11 shows; it denies that bread is life's final ground. 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test' does not forbid trusting God for protection; it forbids demanding a sign to prove His faithfulness. And the devil's quotation of Psalm 91 shows that a verse can be true in itself and still be wrongly used. Believers are not told to quote verses at the enemy like charms, but to know what God has said in its whole context, so that a half-quotation cannot pass for the whole word.

debates.question: Were the temptations physical events or a vision?

views.label: Real, bodily temptations
views.case: Matthew narrates concrete movements, hunger, the temple pinnacle, a mountain, and treats them as genuine external assaults the Son truly resisted in the flesh.

views.label: Partly visionary in mode
views.case: Some hold that seeing all the kingdoms of the world at once suggests a visionary element, though the reality and force of the temptations are in no way diminished.

debates.bearing: Whether experienced bodily or in vision, the temptations were real and really resisted; Jesus' sinless victory stands either way.

debates.question: What was the deepest aim of the three temptations?

views.label: To seize messianic glory without the cross
views.case: Bread, spectacle, and kingdoms offer the crown by shortcut, tempting Jesus to bypass suffering; each answer keeps Him on the Father's path that leads through the cross.

views.label: To make the Son distrust and test the Father
views.case: The refrain if You are the Son of God targets Jesus' trust in the Father's word just spoken at the baptism, tempting Him to prove or doubt rather than simply trust.

debates.bearing: Both aims are one: to divert the Son from faithful obedience; Jesus defeats them by trusting the Father and refusing any road to glory but His.

debates.question: Why do Matthew and Luke put the second and third temptations in a different order?

views.label: Matthew keeps the original order
views.case: Matthew's repeated 'then' and 'again' mark a sequence, and the mountain scene ends with 'Away from Me, Satan!' which sounds like a conclusion. The movement from private need to temple to kingdoms also climbs naturally, and some think Matthew gives the sequence of events.

views.label: Luke keeps the original order
views.case: Luke's chain of 'and' leaves the order looser, and he ends at Jerusalem, the city that frames his Gospel, Luke 4:9 and 9:51. Some argue the temple scene fits his own concerns, so that his order may be the historical one.

views.label: Each writer arranges for his own purpose
views.case: Ancient historians were free to order scenes by theme. Matthew's mountain ending echoes the other mountains in his Gospel, Matthew 5:1 and 28:16-18, while Luke's temple ending points toward Jerusalem.

debates.bearing: The three temptations and the three Scripture answers are the same in both Gospels. Nothing in the teaching depends on which scene was second, and a reader can gain from each writer's arrangement without forcing one onto the other.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the passage, anechthe, 'was led up,' is a passive of anago. Matthew does not say the Spirit 'drove' Jesus, as Mark does with a stronger verb, Mark 1:12. He says Jesus was led, and he adds that it was 'by the Spirit,' so that the test is God's plan, not an accident. The purpose is given by an infinitive, peirasthenai, 'to be tempted,' and the agent of the testing is 'the devil.' God sends Jesus into the test; the devil makes it a temptation. The two intentions meet in a single event, much as God handed Job over to Satan's testing, Job 1:12.

The devil is called ho peirazon, 'the tempter,' in verse 3. It is a participle that names what he does, as Paul does when he fears 'the tempter' may have tempted the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians 3:5. The word 'devil,' diabolos, comes from a verb meaning to throw across, and so to slander. 'Satan,' used by Jesus in verse 10, is a Hebrew word for 'adversary,' as in Zechariah 3:1. Jesus' command, 'Away,' is the single word hypage, the same verb He uses when He sends the demons off in Matthew 8:32. With Peter in Matthew 16:23 He says 'Get behind Me,' a different phrase for a different offence.

The devil's 'If You are the Son of God' is worded as a condition that takes the sonship for granted. The Greek does not say 'since' and does not say 'perhaps'; it sets the voice of Matthew 3:17 in front of Jesus and invites Him to prove it. Compare the crowd at the cross, 'If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!' Matthew 27:40.

In verse 6 the devil quotes Psalm 91:11-12, but he leaves out the words 'to guard you in all your ways.' The omitted phrase confines the promise to the path of obedience. The verb in Jesus' answer, ekpeirazo, 'you shall not put to the test,' is a strengthened form of the verb for tempting, and it quotes Deuteronomy 6:16, which looks back to Massah, where Israel asked, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Exodus 17:7.

In verse 9 the devil says, 'if you will fall down and worship me.' The Greek pairs a participle of falling with the verb proskyneo, so the offer is for an act of full prostration, the posture of a subject before a king. Jesus' answer in verse 10 quotes Deuteronomy 6:13, where the BSB reads 'Fear the LORD your God, serve Him only.' Matthew's wording uses 'worship' and 'serve,' showing that both homage and service belong to God alone.

The closing verb, 'ministered,' is diakoneo, which is the root of our word deacon. It is imperfect, a continuing service, and it is the verb Jesus uses of His own calling, 'not to be served, but to serve,' Matthew 20:28.

typology.type: Adam in the garden, Jesus in the desert
typology.fulfillment: Adam was tempted in a garden of plenty and fell; Jesus is tempted in a wasteland of hunger and stands. Paul draws the line when he calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come,' Romans 5:14, and sets the obedience of one man against the disobedience of another, Romans 5:19. The serpent's question in Genesis 3:1 becomes the devil's 'If You are the Son of God,' and the forbidden fruit becomes bread, a stunt and a throne. The type is surpassed because Jesus does more than avoid Adam's mistake: His obedience becomes the righteousness given to the many. It falls short only in that Adam was a creature at the beginning, while Jesus meets the enemy as the Son Himself.

Israel was God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22, and spent forty years in the wilderness being humbled and tested, Deuteronomy 8:2. Jesus spends forty days there. Every answer He gives is drawn from Moses' review of those years, and each matches a failure: hunger answered by manna and complaint, testing at Massah, and idols at Sinai. Matthew has already told us the nation's story is repeated in Jesus, since He came out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15. He is the faithful Son in whom Israel's calling is completed. The correspondence has limits, because Israel's wandering took a generation and ended in a promised land, while Jesus' trial ends in a battle that continues to the cross.

typology.type: Moses and Elijah, fasting on the mountain
typology.fulfillment: Moses fasted forty days when he received the covenant words, Exodus 34:28, and Elijah went forty days to Horeb, 1 Kings 19:8. Both were given the word of God in a place of hunger. Jesus joins them, but with a difference: He is not about to receive a law from God, He is the One who will give the law on a mountain, Matthew 5:1-2. Moses and Elijah later stand with Him in glory, Matthew 17:3. They show that a man can be sustained by God's word without bread; Jesus shows that He is the one the word is about, and that He keeps it without any lapse, which neither prophet could claim.

typology.type: The angels who serve the Son
typology.fulfillment: The devil cites angels who will lift up the Son; at the end the angels do come, but to serve Him after He has refused the spectacle, verse 11. The Father's care arrives in His own time and way. The angels' ministry echoes Elijah's angel-provided bread, 1 Kings 19:5-8, and Hebrews 1:14 speaks of angels as spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. The picture is also a promise: in Gethsemane the Father could send more than twelve legions, Matthew 26:53, yet the Son chooses the cup. The type falls short in that the angels' care here is brief relief, while the final vindication is the resurrection.

study.christ:
The temptation shows who Jesus is by showing what He refuses. Each of the three offers comes down to an offer of a Messiah without a cross. Bread by a word would make Him a provider of comfort with no need to suffer. A leap from the temple would make Him a wonder-worker who forces the world to believe. The kingdoms by bowing would make Him a ruler without a throne of sacrifice. Satan does not try to make Jesus bad in the ordinary sense; he tries to make Him messianic on the wrong terms. Jesus, who could have turned stones to bread, will later feed thousands with a few loaves, Matthew 14:19, but only on the Father's timing and for others, never to rescue Himself.

The temptations do not end in the wilderness. They return in Matthew's later chapters. Peter's attempt to turn Jesus from the cross draws the same rebuke, 'Get behind Me, Satan!' Matthew 16:23. At the cross the mockers say, 'come down from the cross,' Matthew 27:40. The Gethsemane prayer, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, is the same choice in its darkest hour.

The goal Satan offered is one Jesus receives by obedience. At the end of the Gospel He says, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18, and He meets His disciples on a mountain, the place where the devil had offered Him the world. The kingdoms are not forgotten; they are given at the right price, by the right Father, to the right Son. In Psalm 2:8 the Father says, 'Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance.' Jesus will wait for it.

His victory is real, and it is for us. The Son of God was revealed 'to destroy the works of the devil,' 1 John 3:8, and at the cross He disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:15. Meanwhile Hebrews tells us that He sympathizes with our weakness because He 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. His obedience also counts for those who trust Him, Romans 5:19.

One caution keeps the reading honest. The passage is not mainly a story about how to win against temptation, with Jesus as a model for our technique; it is first an account of what the Son did that we could not. We may follow His example, but we do so as people who have first been given His victory.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows is a God who tests and a God who does not tempt. The Spirit leads Jesus to be tested, and Matthew gives no suggestion that the Father is the author of evil. James says God 'cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself tempts no one,' James 1:13, and the opening verse can be read alongside that. The testing is purposeful, to prove the Son's faithfulness before public ministry begins; the temptation belongs to the devil. God works through the devil's malice for His own ends, as He did when He allowed Job's testing.

The passage shows a God whose word is sufficient. Jesus does not need a new revelation to meet the enemy; He draws on what God has already said, and finds it enough. Deuteronomy 8:3 says man lives 'on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.' That is a claim about how reality works: life is held in being by a speaking God, and trust in that speech is the right response to want.

It shows a God who is faithful beyond what we can see in a given moment. The Father had declared His delight in the Son at the Jordan, and the next scene looks very much like abandonment: hunger, solitude, an enemy. Yet the Father has not left Him. The angels come at the end, and the whole account is a lesson that God's love is not measured by comfort.

It shows God's exclusive claim on worship. The devil offers all the kingdoms; Jesus answers that worship and service belong to the Lord alone, Deuteronomy 6:13. God's glory is not shared with a rival, and a kingdom received from a lesser lord is worth nothing. This is also a statement about God's sovereignty. The kingdoms are not the devil's to give in the final sense; Luke records him saying that they have been relinquished to him, Luke 4:6, but the enemy is a liar, and the Father is the one who gives the nations to the Son, Psalm 2:8.

It shows a God who stoops to His people. In Jesus the Father enters the place of weakness and trial, and so shares what we face, Hebrews 2:18. For worship, this passage invites us to praise a God who is worth more than bread, who needs no testing by our demands, who alone deserves our service, and who has sent a Son through the very pressures that unsettle us.

crossReferences.note: The source of the first answer. Moses tells Israel that God led them forty years in the wilderness to humble and test them, and gave manna so they would learn that man does not live on bread alone. Jesus is led into the wilderness and refuses to feed Himself, taking the lesson Israel failed to learn.

The source of the third answer. Moses commands Israel to fear the LORD, serve Him only and swear by His name, just before they enter a land full of rival gods. Jesus quotes it to the one who offers Him every kingdom and shows that the first commandment is the ground of His kingship.

The source of the second answer: 'Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah.' The command points back to Exodus 17:7, where Israel demanded proof. Jesus refuses to treat a promise as a stage on which God must perform.

The verses the devil quotes at the temple. The psalm promises that angels will bear up the one who trusts the LORD. Matthew's quotation omits the words 'to guard you in all your ways,' so the promise is detached from obedience. The passage shows how a true verse can be used for a false purpose.

The first temptation story, which Matthew's account answers point by point. The woman saw that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes and desirable for wisdom; here the offers also touch appetite, display and power. Adam and Eve, with every tree available, fell; Jesus, with nothing to eat, stands.

The author says Jesus 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' so that we can come to the throne of grace with confidence. The wilderness is the opening of that experience: He knows hunger, doubt of the Father's care and the lure of a quick kingdom from the inside.

The scene Jesus recalls with the word 'test.' Israel was thirsty at Rephidim and demanded water, and Moses named the place Massah and Meribah because they tested the LORD, asking, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' The devil's temple demand has the same shape, a request to prove that God is present.

The baptism that sets the scene. The Spirit descends, and the Father declares, 'This is My beloved Son.' The devil's twice-repeated 'If You are the Son of God' is aimed straight at this declaration. Jesus' answer is to rest on the word that was spoken, not to demand a sign of it.

Luke's version carries the same three temptations, with the temple scene third and the ending that the devil 'left Him until an opportune time.' That line warns the reader that the contest is not over, and it prepares for the cross, where the same voice is heard again.

Paul reads Israel's wilderness as a warning to the church, listing their testing of God, their idolatry and their grumbling. He closes with the promise that God will not let believers be tempted beyond what they can bear. Jesus walks through the same test and does not fall, so the way out Paul promises is found in Him.

James says, 'Submit yourselves to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.' The temptation shows the pattern at its fullest: Jesus submits to the Father's word and the devil leaves, verse 11. The believer's resistance is possible because it follows His.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a man in a garden who is told what to eat and what to leave alone, and it follows with the first lie, 'Did God really say?' Genesis 3:1. Every later part of the story carries the shadow of that moment. Israel is called out of Egypt to be God's son and is tested in the desert, and her record is one of grumbling, testing and idols. By the time of Matthew, the people are back under foreign rule, and the questions of Genesis 3 have not been settled. Who will be the faithful man? Who will be the faithful Israel?

Matthew 4 is the answer in a single scene. The beloved Son goes where Adam fell and Israel failed, and wins by the word of God. He does not do it in a garden of plenty but in a place of hunger, with every reason to take a short way out. The victory is the first stroke of a campaign. It leads on to the Galilean ministry, where He heals the sick and drives out demons, which shows the strong man being bound, Matthew 12:28-29. It leads to the cross, where the old tempter's voice returns through mocking lips, and to the resurrection, where the Son receives the authority the devil offered, Matthew 28:18.

The temptation also sets the pattern for His people. They are united to Him and called to obey the same Father in the same way, by trusting His word, refusing to test Him and giving worship only to Him. They meet the same enemy, and they know the outcome in advance, because 'the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet,' Romans 16:20.

The end of the story is the full reversal of this scene. In the new creation the tempter is gone, thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10, and the kingdoms of the world 'have become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' Revelation 11:15. The Son who refused the shortcut receives the nations, and those who followed Him through trial reign with Him.

quiz.q: Who led Jesus into the wilderness, and why?

options.text: The Spirit led Him there to be tested by the devil.
options.note: Verse 1 says the Spirit led Him to be tempted by the devil.

options.text: Jesus withdrew there on His own to fast and pray.
options.note: He did fast, but the text says the Spirit led Him there for the purpose of testing.

options.text: The devil dragged Him there against His will.
options.note: The Spirit led Him; the devil came to tempt, but did not compel Him into the wilderness.

options.text: John the Baptist sent Him into the desert.
options.note: It was the Spirit, not John, who led Jesus into the wilderness.

quiz.q: How did Jesus respond to each temptation?

options.text: He answered each time with Scripture, quoting from Deuteronomy.
options.note: All three replies begin It is written and cite Deuteronomy 6 to 8.

options.text: He rebuked the devil with His own divine authority.
options.note: He does finally say Away from Me, Satan, but His consistent weapon was the written word of God.

options.text: He performed a miracle to prove His power.
options.note: He refused to work miracles at the devil's prompting; He answered with Scripture.

options.text: He remained silent and simply endured.
options.note: He spoke, answering each temptation with a specific verse.

quiz.q: What did the third temptation offer, and what was its price?

options.text: All the kingdoms of the world, if Jesus would fall down and worship Satan.
options.note: Verses 8-9 record the offer of the kingdoms in exchange for worshiping the devil.

options.text: Rescue by angels, if He would leap from the temple.
options.note: That was the second temptation; the third offered the kingdoms for worship of Satan.

options.text: Bread and comfort, if He would end His fast.
options.note: That relates to the first temptation; the third concerned the world's kingdoms.

options.text: Long life, if He would abandon His mission quietly.
options.note: The offer was the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship, not long life.

quiz.q: How does Jesus succeed where Adam and Israel failed?

options.text: As the true Israel and new Adam, He trusts and obeys God's word under testing.
options.note: His forty days and Deuteronomy quotations frame Him as the faithful Son who does not fall.

options.text: He simply had more willpower than they did.
options.note: It was faithful trust in and obedience to God's word, not mere willpower, that won the day.

options.text: He avoided temptation altogether by leaving the wilderness.
options.note: He did not avoid it; He faced and defeated it there.

options.text: He was never really tempted, only appearing to be.
options.note: The temptations were real; Hebrews says He was tempted in every way, yet without sin.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus refuse the devil's shortcuts to glory?

options.text: He chose the Father's path of obedient suffering rather than a crown gained by compromise.
options.note: Each temptation offered glory without the cross, which Jesus rejected.

options.text: He did not want the kingdoms of the world at all.
options.note: He is destined to receive the kingdoms, but from the Father by the way of the cross, not from the devil.

options.text: He was not yet powerful enough to accept them.
options.note: The issue was faithfulness, not a lack of power.

options.text: He doubted that the devil could deliver on the offer.
options.note: He refused on the ground of worshiping God alone, not because he questioned the offer.

questions: Jesus met every temptation with the word of God. How well do you know the Scriptures you would need in your own moments of testing, and how might you hide more of God's word in your heart?
The tempter's refrain was if You are the Son of God, an attack on Jesus' trust in the Father's love just declared at His baptism. Where does the enemy tempt you to doubt what God has said about you?
Each temptation offered a shortcut to something good by a wrong path. Where are you tempted to reach a good goal by a way that dishonors God?
Jesus insisted that worship and service belong to God alone. What rivals for that exclusive worship are competing for your heart right now?
After the trial, angels came and ministered to Jesus. How does it encourage you that God sustains His people in and after their testing?

translationNotes.note: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3, the lesson Israel was meant to learn in the wilderness, that they live by every word from God's mouth.
The devil quotes Psalm 91:11-12, but misapplies it; Scripture can be twisted, and Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:16 against putting God to the test.
Away from Me, Satan and the citation of Deuteronomy 6:13 name the devil plainly and settle that worship belongs to God alone.
